01.note: Rav Safra told Abaye about a scholar from the Land of Israel, Rav Avira, who reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had declared an animal a tereifa because of a needle found sticking out of only one side of its stomach wall. Abaye sent for him; Rav Avira did not come, so Abaye went to him. Rav Avira was standing on a roof and would not come down, so Abaye climbed up and asked what had actually happened. Rav Avira said he had been present: Rabbi turned the stomach wall over, found a drop of blood on the outside, and ruled it a tereifa, asking where the blood could come from if there was no wound there. Abaye retorted that he had been troubled for nothing, since this is simply the mishna's rule about a stomach perforated to the outside.
01.why: The Gemara has been discussing needles found in an animal's stomach and how a drop of blood shows a wound came before slaughter. Rav Avira's report seemed to clash with the rule that a needle makes an animal a tereifa only if it pierces right through.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: The Sage who tells Abaye about the visiting scholar's report.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who goes to great lengths to question Rav Avira, then finds the case adds nothing new.

people.name: Rav Avira
people.about: A Torah scholar from the Land of Israel who says he witnessed the ruling; he refuses to come down from the roof.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called 'Rabbi' and 'the Great Rabbi'; the teacher who inspected the animal and ruled on it.

people.name: Rav Huna of Tzippori
people.about: One of two scholars Rav Avira says were sitting before Rabbi when the case came up.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect. Its meat is forbidden to eat even if it was slaughtered properly.
One of the chambers of a cow's or sheep's stomach; its wall is thick, so a needle can lodge inside it.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments. Here it lists stomach perforations that make an animal a tereifa.
Rav Avira's description of his job in the study hall; it explains why he was standing near Rabbi and saw the case himself.

02.note: A young goat belonging to Ravina saw barley groats through an open skylight, jumped through it and fell from the roof to the ground. The case came before Rav Ashi. Ravina asked him why Rav Huna rules that an animal left on a roof and found below need not be checked for shattered limbs: is it because animals usually have something to grab on the way down, which this goat did not, or because an animal judges for itself whether it can make the jump, which this goat also did? Rav Ashi answered that it is because the animal judges itself, and this goat did so too.
02.why: The mishna says an animal that fell from a roof is a tereifa, and Rav Huna has just limited that to falls nobody saw happen. Ravina's goat tests the reason behind Rav Huna's leniency.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Owner of the young goat; he puts the question to Rav Ashi.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage the case came before; he rules that the goat need not be suspected of injury.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage whose earlier ruling about animals found below a roof Ravina asks about.

terms.meaning: Internal crushing injuries from a fall. If suspected, the animal may be a tereifa, an animal with a fatal defect whose meat is forbidden.

03.note: A bull fell in the slaughterhouse, and its bellowing from the blow could be heard. Even so, Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta went in and took some of the very best cuts of its meat. The Sages asked him how he knew this was allowed. He answered with a teaching of Rav: when a bull falls, it digs in its hooves until it reaches the ground.
03.why: Rav Naḥman has just ruled that an animal thrown down in the slaughterhouse is not suspected of shattered limbs. This incident shows the ruling applied even to a fall loud enough to hear.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta
people.about: The Sage who took the best meat of the fallen bull without worry and explained why.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose teaching about how a bull falls Rav Yitzḥak quotes.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect, such as crushed internal organs from a bad fall. Its meat is forbidden even if properly slaughtered.

04.note: In the house of Rav Kahana, a cat chased a hen into a small room. The door shut in the cat's face, and the cat struck the door with its paws in anger. Afterward five drops of blood, which the Gemara understands as the cat's venom, were found on the door.
04.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a cat's claw is venomous enough to make a small animal a tereifa only when bystanders try to save the prey. The hen incident is raised as a challenge, since the cat produced venom with no one there to save the hen.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage in whose house the hen was kept.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect; its meat is forbidden even if properly slaughtered. A predator's venomous clawing can make an animal one.

05.note: In the house of Rav Kahana, a cat chased a hen into a small room. The door shut in the cat's face, and the cat struck the door with its paws in anger. Afterward five drops of blood, which the Gemara understands as the cat's venom, were found on the door. The Gemara answers that for a cat, saving itself counts the same as when others try to save its prey.
05.why: In the second version of the debate, the view that a cat's claw is venomous only when someone is there to save the prey is challenged by this incident. The Gemara's answer keeps that view standing.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage in whose house the hen was kept.

terms.meaning: Bystanders trying to rescue an animal from a predator. One view holds that this angers the predator so that its claws become venomous.

06.note: A basket of birds came before Rav. A hawk had got in among them, and it was uncertain whether it had clawed them. Rav sent the birds to Shmuel, and Shmuel strangled them and threw them into the river.
06.why: Rav and Shmuel disagree on whether a possible clawing must be treated as real. The Gemara suggests this case shows Rav retracted and came round to Shmuel; the discussion then rejects that, saying Rav sent the birds because it was Shmuel's town.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage the birds were first brought to; he passed them on to Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who strangled the birds and threw them in the river.

terms.meaning: Attacked by a predator's claws. A bird clawed by a hawk is treated as a tereifa, an animal with a fatal injury whose meat is forbidden.

07.note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana was walking in the desert and found some rams whose lungs were shriveled. He came and asked in the study hall what to do. The Sages told him how to test such lungs: in summer, put them in white vessels of cold water for twenty-four hours, and in winter in dark vessels of tepid water. If the lungs return to looking healthy, the shriveling was from Heaven and the animals are kosher; if not, they are tereifa. The text does not say what he found when he tested them.
07.why: The mishna rules that a lung shriveled by the hand of Heaven is kosher, while a baraita says one shriveled by a person's doing is a tereifa. This story gives the practical test for telling the two apart.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: The Sage who found the rams in the desert and brought the question to the study hall.

terms.meaning: From natural causes rather than from something a person did; for example, a lung shriveled by fright at thunder.
An animal with a fatal defect; its meat is forbidden even if it was slaughtered properly.

08.note: A hen in the house of Rav Ḥana had a head injury, and he sent it to Rav Mattana. Rav Mattana found that the skull bone was broken but the membrane of the brain was not pierced, and he ruled it kosher. Rav Ḥana objected with Levi's teaching that a bird whose skull is broken is a tereifa even if the membrane is intact. Rav Mattana answered that Levi meant a water bird, because its membrane is fragile.
08.why: The Gemara is asking whether a bird with a broken skull can be inspected and permitted, given Levi's teaching. The same objection and answer have just appeared between Rav Naḥman and Rav Anan; this case shows the answer applied to a real hen.

people.name: Rav Ḥana
people.about: Owner of the injured hen; he challenges Rav Mattana's ruling.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: The Sage who inspected the hen and ruled it kosher.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage whose teaching lists the defects that make a bird forbidden.

terms.meaning: The thin covering around the brain. If it is pierced, the bird is forbidden; the question is whether a broken skull alone is enough.
An animal or bird with a fatal defect; its meat is forbidden even if properly slaughtered.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

09.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had a hen that fell into the fire. He sent it to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, telling him its innards had turned green, and Rabbi Elazar HaKappar ruled it kosher. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi objected that the mishna says green innards make a bird unfit. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar answered that the rule applies only to the gizzard, the heart and the liver.
09.why: The mishna rules that a bird that fell into a fire is a tereifa if its innards turned green. This case limits that rule to the organs that are normally red, and the Gemara backs the answer with a baraita.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Owner of the hen; he questions the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
people.about: Called 'the distinguished'; the Sage who ruled the hen kosher.

terms.meaning: Forbidden to eat because of a fatal defect, the status called tereifa.
A muscular stomach in birds that grinds food.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

10.note: Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Yosef had a hen that fell into the fire, and he sent it to Rabbi Abbahu. Its innards were red, yet it was ruled a tereifa. Rabbi Yitzḥak objected that the mishna says red innards are kosher. The answer was that red innards that turned green, and green innards that turned red, make a bird a tereifa; the mishna's rule that red is kosher applies only to the heart, the gizzard and the liver.
10.why: It is the companion to the case just told, where green innards were permitted. Together they show that the mishna's color test for a bird that fell into fire depends on each organ's natural color.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Yosef
people.about: Owner of the hen; he questions the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage the hen was sent to.

terms.meaning: An animal or bird with a fatal defect; its meat is forbidden even if properly slaughtered.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

10.flag: The hen is sent to Rabbi Abbahu, but the English translation credits the ruling and answer to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, which the Aramaic does not name; the note avoids naming who ruled.

11.note: A Roman saw a man fall from a roof to the ground; his belly burst open and his intestines came out. The Roman brought the man's son and slaughtered him in front of him, but only as an illusion. The father fainted and went limp, his intestines slipped back inside, and the Roman sewed up his belly.
11.why: The mishna says a bird whose intestines came out but were not pierced stays kosher, and a Sage adds that organs have fixed places and must go back in order. The story shows intestines returning to their place in a man.

people.name: the Roman
people.about: An unnamed Roman who stages the trick and sews up the injured man.

12.note: A young deer was brought to the house of the Exilarch, its hind legs cut. Rav examined the sinews of its thigh, found them intact and ruled it kosher, and he meant to eat it lightly roasted. Shmuel asked him whether he was not worried it might have been bitten by a snake. When Rav asked what could be done, Shmuel said to put it in a hot oven, where it would test itself. He did, and the meat fell off in pieces. Shmuel applied to Rav the verse 'No mischief shall befall the righteous,' and Rav applied to Shmuel the verse 'No secret causes you trouble.'
12.why: The mishna, as the Gemara cites it, says an animal bitten by a snake is not a tereifa but is still forbidden because it is dangerous. The incident shows how that danger was detected; it also follows a run of warnings about foods that harm the body.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who inspected the deer, ruled it kosher and planned to eat it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who suspected a snakebite and proposed the oven test.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful leader in whose household Sages often ate and ruled.
The place in the thigh where the tendons meet; if they are intact, an animal with injured legs can still be kosher.
Permitted to eat under Jewish law.

13.note: In the house of the Exilarch a karkoz goat was slaughtered, and a whole basket of fat was taken from it. Rav Aḥai declared the fat forbidden, but Rav Shmuel, son of Rabbi Abbahu, ate some of it and applied to himself the verse 'A man's belly shall be filled with the fruit of his mouth.' The Sages of the Land of Israel sent word that the law follows Rav Shmuel, son of Rabbi Abbahu, but that people should be mindful of Rav Aḥai's honor, because he lights up the eyes of the exile.
13.why: The Gemara has just set out the signs on the horns that mark an animal as wild, whose fat is permitted, rather than domesticated, whose fat is forbidden. The karkoz goat was the uncertain case those signs left open.

people.name: Rav Aḥai
people.about: The Sage who forbade the fat; the Sages of the Land of Israel praise him as one who lights up the eyes of the exile.

people.name: Rav Shmuel, son of Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage who ate the fat, trusting his own learning; the law was ruled to follow him.

terms.meaning: A kind of goat whose status was in doubt: was it a domesticated animal or a wild one?
Certain fats of domesticated animals such as cattle, sheep and goats are forbidden by the Torah; the same fats of wild animals are permitted.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, in whose household this goat was slaughtered.

14.note: The Roman emperor told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya that his God is compared to a lion, yet a horseman can kill a lion. Rabbi Yehoshua said God is compared to the lion of Bei Ila'ei. The emperor insisted on seeing it, so Rabbi Yehoshua prayed and the lion set out. Four hundred parasangs away it roared once: pregnant women miscarried and the wall of Rome fell. At three hundred it roared again: men's teeth fell out, and the emperor fell from his throne. He begged Rabbi Yehoshua to pray it back, and it returned. Another time the emperor asked to see God. Rabbi Yehoshua stood him facing the summer sun, and when he could not look, said: if you cannot look at one of God's servants, all the more so the Divine Presence.
14.why: Rav Yehuda has just identified an animal from a list of kosher and forbidden beasts as the lion of Bei Ila'ei, and Rav Kahana has described its enormous size. The story about that lion follows, and a second exchange with the same emperor is told after it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya
people.about: The Sage who answers the emperor's challenges and prays to bring the lion and send it back.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman emperor who mocks the comparison of God to a lion and demands to see first the lion, then God.

terms.meaning: A giant lion from a place called Bei Ila'ei; the Gemara says it measured nine cubits between its ears.
A Persian measure of distance, roughly four miles.
God's presence in the world, called the Shekhina.
A Hebrew month in midsummer, when the sun is at its strongest.

14.flag: The span joins two separate exchanges between the emperor and Rabbi Yehoshua (the lion of Bei Ila'ei, and the request to see God); each could stand as its own story.

15.note: The Roman emperor told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya that he wanted to prepare a meal for his God. Rabbi Yehoshua said he could not, because God's hosts are too many. The emperor insisted, so Rabbi Yehoshua told him to set it out on the shore of the great sea, where there is open space. The emperor worked for the six months of summer, and a wind swept it all into the sea; he worked the six months of winter, and rain sank it all into the sea. When he asked what this was, Rabbi Yehoshua said these were only the sweepers and floor washers who serve God. The emperor admitted that he could not do it.
15.why: It is one of a series of exchanges between the Roman emperor and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya that the Gemara strings together, each showing the emperor that God's greatness is beyond him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya
people.about: The Sage who tells the emperor how and where to prepare the meal.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman emperor who wants to host a meal for the God of Israel.

16.note: The Roman emperor's daughter told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya that his God must be a carpenter, quoting a verse about God laying the beams of His upper chambers in the waters, and asked him to tell God to make her a distaff. He agreed and prayed, and she was struck with leprosy. She was seated in the Roman market and given a distaff, since Romans gave one to every leper so that people would see and pray for them. One day Rabbi Yehoshua passed by and asked whether she liked the distaff his God had given her. She told him to ask his God to take back what He had given. He replied that our God gives but does not take back.
16.why: It continues the run of exchanges between the Roman emperor's household and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya, each turning a mocking challenge about God back on the one who made it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya
people.about: The Sage who prays for the emperor's daughter and later speaks with her in the market.

people.name: the emperor's daughter
people.about: The daughter of the Roman emperor, who mocks God as a carpenter and asks for a distaff.

terms.meaning: A simple stick used in spinning, holding the wool or flax that is drawn off into thread.
The translation's word for a serious skin disease; in Rome, according to the story, sufferers sat in the market to draw people's prayers.

17.note: Rav Naḥman bar Pappa had a garden. He planted seeds, but they did not sprout. He prayed, rain came, and they sprouted. He said that this is what Rav Asi had taught.
17.why: Rav Asi has just explained that the grass created on the third day waited at the surface until Adam prayed for rain, because God desires the prayers of the righteous. Rav Naḥman bar Pappa's garden is that teaching borne out in his own life.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Pappa
people.about: The Sage whose garden sprouted only after he prayed.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Rav Naḥman bar Pappa says his garden confirmed.

18.note: A bear attacked a ben pekua belonging to Adda bar Ḥavu, and he came to Rav Ashi, who told him to go and slaughter it. Adda bar Ḥavu objected that Ze'eiri, quoting Rabbi Ḥanina, rules like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, who permits such an animal without slaughter, and that even Rabbi Yoḥanan disagreed only about its offspring. Rav Ashi said Rabbi Yoḥanan was only explaining Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's view. Adda bar Ḥavu pressed on with another report that the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri wherever the Mishna quotes him. Rav Ashi said he holds with Rabbi Yonatan, who follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri only for a man dangerously ill and for teruma of the tithe of demai.
18.why: The Gemara has just quoted Ze'eiri's ruling that a ben pekua needs no slaughter even after it has walked on the ground. This case shows Rav Ashi refusing to follow that ruling, and the Gemara then explains the two cases where he does follow Rabbi Shimon Shezuri.

people.name: Adda bar Ḥavu
people.about: Owner of the animal attacked by the bear; he argues with Rav Ashi's ruling.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who tells Adda bar Ḥavu to slaughter the animal and defends that ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
people.about: An early Sage who permits a ben pekua, and its offspring, without slaughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage whose statement about the offspring of a ben pekua the two argue over.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: The Sage whose limited acceptance of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri Rav Ashi adopts.

terms.meaning: A calf or lamb found alive inside its mother when she was slaughtered. Its mother's slaughter may make it permitted, so whether it needs its own slaughter is debated.
The portion of the Levites' tithe that had to be given to a priest.
Produce bought from someone who might not have separated the required tithes.

19.note: Ulla told Rav Naḥman of an incident he knew of: a young bird in the house of Rabbi Yitzḥak had a broken leg, where skin and flesh together covered the bone. Rabbi Yitzḥak brought it to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who ruled it kosher. Rav Naḥman replied that a young bird is different, because its skin is soft.
19.why: The Gemara is debating what Rabbi Yoḥanan ruled about a broken bone sticking out: whether skin counts together with flesh in covering most of it. Ulla offers this incident as his evidence, and Rav Naḥman pushes it aside.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident as the source for his account of Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage who challenges Ulla and dismisses the incident as a special case.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak
people.about: Owner of the young bird; he brought it to Rabbi Yoḥanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage who ruled the young bird kosher.

terms.meaning: Permitted to eat under Jewish law; here, not made forbidden by the broken leg.

20.note: An animal's leg bone broke and stuck out, and a small piece of it had come away. The case came before Abaye, who put off answering until three pilgrimage festivals had passed. Rav Adda bar Mattana told the owner to go to Rava, son of Rav Yosef bar Ḥama, whose knife is sharp. The owner went, and Rava said: since the rule speaks of a bone that broke and stuck out, what difference does it make whether a piece fell off or stayed in place?
20.why: The Gemara is working through a baraita that permits an animal whose broken bone sticks out, as long as skin and flesh cover most of it. This case asks whether a missing chip of bone changes that, and Rava's answer treats it as the same.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the case first came to; he delayed for three festivals.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: The Sage who sent the owner to Rava.

people.name: Rava, son of Rav Yosef bar Ḥama
people.about: A Sage described as having a sharp knife, quick and incisive in ruling; he decides the case.

terms.meaning: Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, when crowds gathered; Abaye waited for them so he could ask the assembled Sages.
An idiom for a scholar who cuts through legal questions quickly and decisively.
